chief_complaint: retrosternal pressure on exertion, relieved by rest
hpi_details: A 62-year-old male presents to the clinic with retrosternal pressure on exertion, relieved by rest. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: He thinks his chest tightness is just severe acid reflux or a sign of getting older and out of shape.
concerns: He is worried he might collapse and die suddenly from a heart attack while walking alone, just as his father did in his sixties.
expectations: He hopes to have an ECG done to make sure his heart is safe and receive a stronger antacid prescription for his chest discomfort.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Stable Angina is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes assessment for contraindications, noninvasive diagnostic testing, symptom relief with sublingual nitroglycerin when appropriate, and preventive therapy according to confirmed coronary disease and cardiovascular risk, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Stable Angina.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Unstable angina without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Pain at rest — suggests unstable angina.
management_principles: Plan for suspected stable angina: provide sublingual nitroglycerin if appropriate, assess for contraindications, and arrange noninvasive testing; use antiplatelet and statin therapy when coronary artery disease is confirmed or otherwise indicated
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

must_ask.say: Does the pressure happen with exertion?
Does it go away with rest?
How long has this been happening, and is it getting worse?
Do you smoke or have high blood pressure?
Does this ever happen at rest?

history.answer: Whenever I move around or exert myself, I feel a heavy pressure in the center of my chest, but it eases up when I rest.
It started about two weeks ago while I was climbing the stairs at work, and the tightness built up gradually over a couple of minutes.
It feels like a broad pressure right behind my breastbone in the middle of my chest. I cannot point to it with just one finger.
It feels like a heavy squeezing sensation, like a heavy weight pressing down on my chest. It is not sharp or tearing at all.
Sometimes the ache spreads up into the left side of my jaw and down along my left arm.
Each episode lasts about three to five minutes before fading away. It happens once or twice a day whenever I push myself.
When it reaches its peak while I am walking, I would rate it around a five or six out of ten.
Yes, it reliably starts when I walk fast or climb stairs, and sitting down to rest makes it go away completely within a few minutes. It has never happened while I was resting or sleeping.
Over the past two weeks, it has been gradually getting easier to trigger, happening after just one flight of stairs instead of two.
Taking a deep breath, coughing, or bending forward does not change the pressure at all. Pressing on my ribs also does not make it hurt.
It does not happen after meals, lying down does not make it worse, and I have not had any heartburn or trouble swallowing.
I feel a bit short of breath and tired when the pressure comes on, but I have not had any cold sweats, nausea, vomiting, or dizziness.
No, I have not had any fever, chills, cough, or phlegm.
No, I have not had a cold, the flu, or any other illness recently.
No, neither of my legs is swollen or painful, and I have not had surgery, prolonged bed rest, or taken any long flights recently.
No, there are no rashes, blisters, or skin changes anywhere on my chest.
No, I have not had severe panic attacks, a sense of impending doom, or tingling in my hands.
I was diagnosed with high blood pressure and high cholesterol several years ago. I do not have diabetes.
I have never experienced chest tightness like this before these past two weeks, and I have never had any heart tests or stents placed.
No, I have not hit my chest, lifted heavy weights, or strained any chest muscles recently.
I figured it was probably just bad heartburn acting up or that my body is getting out of shape as I get older.
I'm really scared of dropping dead from a sudden heart attack while I'm out walking alone, because that's exactly what happened to my dad.
I was hoping to get an electrocardiogram done to rule out heart damage and maybe get a stronger antacid to settle this chest pressure.
I have had high blood pressure and high cholesterol for about five years, but no other chronic medical conditions.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been admitted to a hospital.
I am not taking any prescribed medications, over-the-counter drugs, or supplements right now.
I have no known allergies to any medications, foods, or other substances.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used tobacco products.
I only drink alcohol socially, usually one or two beers once or twice a month.
I work as an office manager sitting at a desk most of the day, and I live at home with my wife.
My father passed away in his late seventies from natural causes, and my mother had high blood pressure, but no one in my family had early heart disease.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 138/84 mmHg, heart rate is 74 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 16 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation is 98% on room air, and temperature is 36.7 degrees Celsius.
The patient is alert, comfortable at rest, and showing no signs of acute distress, diaphoresis, or pallor.
No rash, erythema, or vesicular lesions are visible across the chest wall.
Jugular venous pressure is normal with no jugular venous distension noted.
Palpation over the sternum, ribs, and costochondral junctions elicits no tenderness and does not reproduce the chest pain.
Normal S1 and S2 heart sounds with regular rate and rhythm, with no murmurs, gallops, or pericardial friction rubs.
Lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally with no crackles, wheezes, or rhonchi.
Percussion is resonant throughout both lung fields.
Abdomen is soft, non-tender to palpation without guarding, rebound tenderness, or organomegaly.
No pitting edema observed in either lower extremity.
Both calves are supple, non-tender, and symmetric without swelling or warmth.
Radial and dorsalis pedis pulses are intact, regular, and symmetric bilaterally.
